analysis.one_liner: Bans doctors from referring Medicare and private-insurance patients to businesses they own for therapy, imaging, and equipment.
analysis.headline: The bill to broaden the ban on physician self-referrals died in House subcommittees and never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already bars doctors from sending Medicare patients to clinical labs they have a financial stake in. This bill would have extended that ban to physical therapy, radiology and imaging, radiation therapy, and medical equipment, and would have applied it to private insurers and state health programs too, not just Medicare. It also tightened some loopholes while writing new exceptions for HMOs and managed care plans. The bill was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees, and no further action was ever taken before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with Medicare, private insurance, or state health coverage, who would be protected from doctors steering them to imaging centers, therapy clinics, or equipment suppliers the doctors profit from. Medicare, private insurers, and state programs would also stop paying claims generated by such self-referrals, since the bill made violative claims unpayable by any payor.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the existing Medicare self-referral ban, previously limited to clinical laboratory services, to physical therapy, radiology and diagnostic imaging, radiation therapy, and durable medical equipment.

Applies the ban to all payors: no payment could be made under Medicare, other federal health programs, state health programs, or by any private third-party payor for designated health services referred in violation of the ban.

Tightens exceptions by replacing the lab-specific rules with a broader 'designated health services' framework, while adding new exceptions for HMOs and certain managed care plans where physicians bear significant financial risk, and directing the Secretary to consider whether valuable community services would be jeopardized without an exception.

analysis.who_pays: Physicians who own or profit from imaging centers, physical therapy and radiation therapy facilities, or durable medical equipment companies would lose the ability to refer patients to those businesses, and would have had to divest existing arrangements (with a two-year grace period) or forgo that revenue.

drawbacks.text: Physicians and hospitals would face new compliance burdens, and the bill gave existing financial relationships a grace period of roughly two years after enactment before the ban applied to them, allowing existing self-referral arrangements to continue during that time.

A good-faith objection is that physician ownership sometimes funds services in markets where no other provider exists; the bill itself acknowledged this by directing the Secretary to consider whether necessary, valuable community services would be jeopardized without an exception.

The new exceptions for HMOs and managed care plans that put physicians at financial risk for service costs preserved a form of physician financial interest in limiting care, which critics of managed care incentives have long pointed to.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit—keeping doctors' personal profits out of decisions about whether patients need an MRI, therapy, or medical equipment—is substantial and directly protects patients and payors from wasted spending. The costs are real but manageable: compliance complexity for providers and a risk of reduced access in some markets, which the bill tried to address through its community-services exception. The two-year grace period weakens the immediate effect but was a practical transition. On balance the design is a reasonable tightening of an existing rule rather than a badly built bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and then to their health subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Kasich introduced the Physician Self-Referral Amendments of 1992 on May 12, 1992, joined by Rep. Rick Santorum as the bill's one cosponsor.
The bill was referred jointly to the House Committees on Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means on the day it was introduced.

Within days it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health and the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, and the record shows no further action for the rest of the Congress.
Congress adjourned on January 3, 1993, and the bill died with no vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Physicians with ownership stakes in imaging, therapy, and medical equipment businesses, and the managed care plans the bill would have newly regulated, are better off because it never advanced; patients and health programs continue to bear the cost of self-referred services.

for.name: Rep. John Kasich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend the self-referral ban to all payors and to imaging, therapy, and equipment services.

for.name: Rep. Rick Santorum
for.role: Original cosponsor, U.S. House of Representatives (R-PA)

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee / Subcommittee on Health
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over Medicare financing
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 12, 1992, sent it to the Subcommittee on Health on May 15, and took no further action on it.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee / Subcommittee on Health and the Environment
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over public health programs
against.what_they_did: Received the joint referral on May 12, 1992, sent it to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment on May 26, and took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by two Republicans with no recorded votes or hearing testimony, so the partisan shape of support and opposition never became visible.

industries.industry: Physician-owned imaging, physical therapy, and radiation therapy facilities
industries.note: The bill would have barred doctors from referring patients for these services to entities the doctors profit from, ending a revenue stream built on the doctor's own referral decision. Patients and insurers currently bear the cost of potentially unnecessary self-referred services.

industries.industry: Durable medical equipment suppliers with physician ownership
industries.note: Furnishing of durable medical equipment would have become a designated health service under the self-referral ban, cutting off physician-owned equipment arrangements.

industries.industry: Private health insurers and state health programs
industries.note: Extending the ban to all payors meant private and state programs could stop paying claims generated by prohibited self-referrals, giving them the same protection Medicare already had.

The bill wrote a new exception allowing HMOs and managed care plans to keep operating with physicians bearing significant financial risk for service costs, locking in managed care's role alongside the new restrictions.
